Facts: Heir challenged brother’s right to inherit based on alleged insults to deceased mother, seeking declaration of unworthiness; also contested validity of mother’s holographic will dated June 17, 2007, claiming testamentary incapacity.
Legal Framework: Art. 463 Civil Code (unworthiness to inherit); Art. 801 Civil Code (revocation for ingratitude); Art. 542 Civil Code (reserved portions); holographic will validity requirements.
Interpretative Issues: Whether insults or offensive behavior toward deceased constitute grounds for unworthiness to inherit; how unworthiness grounds under Art. 463 Civil Code relate to revocation for ingratitude under Art. 801 Civil Code; burden of proof for challenging testamentary capacity.
Legal Principles: Grounds for unworthiness to inherit under Art. 463 Civil Code are exhaustive and strictly construed; they cannot be extended by analogy to include conduct not expressly enumerated in statute. Insults or offensive behavior toward deceased, while potentially constituting ingratitude justifying donation revocation under Art. 801 Civil Code, do not fall within statutory grounds for unworthiness absent specific criminal conduct or acts preventing testamentary freedom. Distinction between unworthiness (operating by law to exclude heir from succession) and revocation for ingratitude (requiring testator’s act during lifetime) must be maintained. Holographic will validity requires proof of testamentary capacity at moment of execution; medical evidence and witness testimony establish capacity. Court confirmed inheritance shares according to valid will: equal portions to some heirs, larger portion to specifically favored heir, reflecting testator’s autonomy in disposing of available portion. ID: ITI096; Instance_Type: First instance; Legal_Duration: P5Y3M; Law: IT – Civil Code – 542(2), 553 ss., 737 ss., 720, 463, 801; State: IT; Type: Succession; Immovable_Assets: House, House, House ; Movable_Assets: Jewelry, Money (100.000,00), Money (144.000,00); Type_of_succession: Testamentary; Second part of full text: FACTUAL AND LEGAL GROUNDS (CONCISE STATEMENT)
HEIR 1 (hereinafter also referred to as 'the plaintiff' or 'HEIR 1') brought legal proceedings against HEIR 2 (hereinafter also referred to as 'HEIR 2'), HEIR 3 (hereinafter also referred to as 'HEIR 3'), HEIR 4 (hereinafter also referred to as "HEIR 4"), and THIRD PARTY 1 (hereinafter also referred to as "THIRD PARTY 1") (collectively referred to as "the defendants") to ascertain and declare HEIR 2's unworthiness to inherit, with an order for the immediate return of all assets and proceeds from the opening of the succession; to uphold the action pursuant to Article 801 of the Italian Civil Code against HEIR 2 for the serious, intolerable and repeated abuse of his mother THE DECEASED as described in the narrative, with the aforementioned defendant being ordered to return to the estate all donations received from his mother during her lifetime, as detailed in the documents; to declare the full validity of the holographic will drawn up by THE DECEASED on 17 June 2017 and subsequently published by the Notary THIRD PARTY 2 of Forlì, as it was drawn up by a person of sound mind, declaring the challenge to the will by HEIR 2 in the settlement agreement of 28 April 2017, ordering HEIR 2 to compensate the plaintiff for all damages for the serious offences directed at the mother, father and the plaintiff himself in the same deed, settling said compensation in the amount of €40,000 or any other higher or lower sum deemed fair pursuant to Article 1226 of the Italian Civil Code; to order HEIR 2 to pay the sum of €100,000.00 or such other sum as may be deemed fair for the sole management of the properties in Via (OMISSIS); to order HEIR 2 to provide an account pursuant to Article 263 of the Italian Civil Code of the rents and utilities received in respect of the two rents highlighted; to ascertain the nature of indirect generosity, for the sum of €144,000.00 or such other sum as may be deemed fair, of the loan for use of the property located at Via (OMISSIS) granted by the mother to her son HEIR 2 for the purposes of fictitious reunification; for the dissolution of the joint ownership of the inheritance with the attribution to the plaintiff of the assets corresponding to his ideal share of co-ownership (equal to 3/16). All with costs.
The plaintiff stated that his mother, THE DECEASED, died on 20 August 2007. In her youth, Ms THE DECEASED had obtained a degree in French language and literature; During the 1950s, she taught in various schools and high schools for about ten years, until she made an agreement with her husband, RELATIVE 1, whereby, in exchange for her wife giving up her teaching career and her contribution to the family and children, as well as the management of family affairs, she would receive various financial payments from her husband.
The marriage produced four children, HEIR 3, HEIR 1, HEIR 4 and HEIR 2, who are the current parties to the case. The marital union continued over time until, in 2005-2006, Mrs THE DECEASED learned that she was suffering from a serious illness, which led to her death after years of surgery and treatment. Until her death, despite her suffering, the deceased remained lucid, although her ability to speak had diminished in recent times.
The deceased left a holographic will, dated 17 June 2007, in which she named her children HEIR 3, HEIR 1, HEIR 4 and HEIR 2 as heirs, assigning to the latter, in addition to the reserved portion, her own disposable portion. The other heirs were immediately informed of the existence of the will by HEIR 3, who, however, waited to publish it, at the request of HEIR 2, pending a settlement of the disputes between the siblings, which never came. Thus, the will was published on 11 January 2013 by Notary THIRD PARTY 2.
The plaintiff pointed out that the defendant HEIR 2 had never contested the will, but had instead given it his full confirmation.
Subsequently, on 26 December 2016, the father and husband of the deceased, RELATIVE 1, also died. Only after the death of the father, on 5 January 2017, did the defendant HEIR 2 express his intention to contest the will of THE DECEASED, claiming that it was voidable.
However, in the plaintiff's opinion, the will was fully valid, as the deceased was fully lucid and aware at the time of drafting the will, given that the deceased's lucidity never waned, despite her illness, and only declined from August 2007, i.e. two months after the will was drafted and shortly before her death. The deceased also attended a party for her daughter-in-law RELATIVE 2's birthday on 28 July 2007, where she sang and conversed with the other guests. The text of the will is clear and unambiguous, as well as logical and conclusive in its content.
The defendant HEIR 2's challenge to the will is completely reckless and likely to result in liability for damages, given the obvious harm caused to his mother, father and brother. The husband and father of the parties, RELATIVE 1, having seen the will, in which he did not appear, renounced his inheritance, thus confirming the validity of the will itself.
Moreover, the deceased's wish to benefit her son HEIR 3 was linked to profound reasons well known to the parties, and the contestation of the will would in any case be covered by the five-year statute of limitations. Finally, there were multiple acts by HEIR 2 confirming recognition of the will and the shares arising from it, as specified in the deeds.
The plaintiff also argued that the defendant HEIR 2 was unworthy of succession; in particular, the act of contesting the will constituted a manifestation of genuine aversion towards his mother, with whom he had always had a conflictual relationship, partly due to a radically different outlook on life. The defendant HEIR 2 had also put forward the absurd and offensive argument that his mother was merely a fictitious owner of her husband's assets, without money or rights, incapable of saving and lacking technical and legal knowledge, all circumstances far from reality, and had also falsely claimed that his mother was incapable of understanding and willing at the time of the will.
In reality, the deceased had left teaching only because of an agreement reached with her husband, which had nothing to do with the donation, but fell within the scope of Article 2034 of the Italian Civil Code, and had therefore devoted herself to caring for her family and also to managing her husband's affairs, in particular his real estate assets. In any case, Ms THE DECEASED also owned her own assets, independently of her husband, jointly with her brothers THIRD PARTY 1 and RELATIVE 3.
That said, the plaintiff expressed his intention to raise 1) a question of constitutional legitimacy and 2) a preliminary ruling on the acts to the EU in relation to Article 463 of the Civil Code.
In particular, in relation to Article 3 of the Constitution, Article 463 of the Civil Code would be unconstitutional insofar as it does not provide for any cause for exclusion from succession the behaviour of the heir prior to or after the death of the deceased, aimed at preventing the fulfilment of the deceased's last wishes, in particular by attempting to delay the publication of the will, through threats and cajoling, and then attempting to contest its validity despite being aware of the perfect legitimacy of the will itself. Furthermore, the legislation would also conflict with the provisions of the EU Treaty and the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.
These requests are aimed at declaring the defendant HEIR 2 unworthy of inheriting from his mother THE DECEASED.
In the alternative, the conditions for revocation on grounds of ingratitude pursuant to Article 801 of the Italian Civil Code of the donations received by HEIR 2 would exist, due to blatant disrespect, contempt, aversion and lack of gratitude towards his mother, all as manifested by the actions described above. The plaintiff then specified in the documents the donations that should be subject to revocation. The conduct of the defendant HEIR 2 would also give rise to liability for damages on his part.
The plaintiff also claimed that, after the death of the deceased, HEIR 2 had managed two apartments, located in Bologna and Madonna di Campiglio, on his own, for which he should be held accountable. In particular, he had held the property in Madonna di Campiglio for about nine years, from winter 2007 to winter/spring 2016, excluding the other siblings. There was never any loan for use of the property in question, as the siblings never had the keys, which were handed over to HEIR 2 by RELATIVE 1 himself, and the other siblings waited in vain for the management account without ever obtaining their share of the related proceeds, which were due to the plaintiff in the amount of 3/16, plus additional damages and interest. In addition, the defendant HEIR 2 should pay the sum of €4,424.00 for expenses incurred for new furniture.
For the property in Via (OMISSIS), the keys were handed over voluntarily by their father RELATIVE 1 to HEIR 2, who kept them until September 2016.
The defendant HEIR 2 also benefited from the free loan of the property in Via (OMISSIS) by his mother THE DECEASED from 1990 to 2002, and must therefore pay the estate the rental value of €144,000.00 or such other sum as may be deemed fair, as this loan constitutes an indirect donation.
As regards the composition of the inheritance shares, according to HEIR 1, the heirs would be entitled to the following shares respectively: 7/16 to HEIR 3, 3/16 to HEIR 2, 3/16 to HEIR 1 and 3/16 to HEIR 4. According to a different hypothesis, given the spouse's renunciation, the children would be considered as if they were the only legitimate heirs, therefore HEIR 3 would be entitled to half of the estate. According to another theory, as the available portion increases due to the spouse's renunciation, HEIR 3 would be entitled to 5/8 of the estate, and the other siblings would be entitled to 1/8 each.
The shares of the assets that, at the time of the deceased's death, were jointly owned by the latter and THIRD PARTY 1, uncle of the other parties to the case, must also be taken into account.
He also claimed that the defendant HEIR 3 had received some properties from his mother through a sale, specifying that any action of simulation aimed at obtaining the collation of these assets would be unfounded and time-barred.
The plaintiff also claimed to have received some donations from his mother, namely €200,000.00 in cash and two properties in (OMISSIS).
He further claimed that HEIR 4 had received donations of cash and securities worth €200,000.00 in addition to the properties indicated in the deeds.
There were also donations to THE DECEASED's grandchildren, which were not subject to reduction in the absence of acceptance of the benefit and were not subject to collation.
The plaintiff then proceeded to list the assets forming part of the estate, proposing a calculation of the respective shares due to the heirs.
THIRD PARTY 1 did not appear in court and was declared in default at the hearing on 4 July 2018.
HEIR 2 appeared in court in a timely manner, concluding that the present case should be joined with the case pending under RG 3958 of 2017, for a declaration of inadmissibility of the claims brought by HEIR 1 on the grounds of vagueness and violation of the requirements of Article 163 bis of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure and, on the merits, for the rejection of the plaintiff's claims as unfounded and reckless, with the plaintiff ordered to pay damages for reckless litigation pursuant to Article 96, paragraph 3, of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, quantified at €200,000.00 or such other sum as may be deemed fair; for the acceptance of the claims brought in civil case no. 3958 of 2017, as specifically transcribed, relating to the revocation for ingratitude of the donations made by RELATIVE 1 and received by HEIR 3 and HEIR 1, for the determination of the estate of RELATIVE 1 and for the assessment of the estate of THE DECEASED, all as indicated in the narrative, for the reduction of donations made in favour of HEIR 1 and HEIR 3, subject to a declaration of simulation of the related apparent real estate sales, with reinstatement of the legitimate rights of the defendant HEIR 2, for the annulment of the will of THE DECEASED pursuant to Article 591, paragraph 2, of the Italian Civil Code, for the division pursuant to Article 713 of the Italian Civil Code between the co-heirs of the deceased lawyer RELATIVE 1 and the deceased THE DECEASED of their respective inheritance shares, subject to collation by the co-heirs of the direct and indirect donations and gifts received as indicated in the deeds, with HEIR 3 ordered to pay the defendant the civil fruits deriving from the assets subject to the concealed donations; for the declaration of forfeiture by HEIR 1 and HEIR 3 of the benefit of inventory with respect to the inheritance of RELATIVE 1; for the order of the co-heirs to reimburse HEIR 2 for the expenses incurred for the common property with reference to the apartments in undivided co-ownership at No. (OMISSIS) of the Condominium (OMISSIS) in Madonna di Campiglio, plus interest and monetary revaluation, in any case determining the fruits and interest on the sums subject to reduction or collation from the opening of the succession to the balance, with the co-heirs and third parties ordered to pay HEIR 2 the corresponding amount.
He then requested that it be ascertained that HEIR 3 had received, prior to the drafting of the will, gifts sufficient to cover the entire estate, thereby infringing on the legitimate rights of HEIR 2; ascertain and declare that the respective inheritance shares amount to 1/4 each, all subject to the failure to ascertain that all the assets of THE DECEASED's estate belong to RELATIVE 1's estate, with the exception of the properties co-owned with his brother THIRD PARTY 1; order the co-owners to reimburse HEIR 2 for all condominium expenses, utilities, maintenance and furnishings of the property in Madonna di Campiglio incurred up to 2016; ascertain and declare the limitation and forfeiture of the claim of alleged ingratitude for acts allegedly committed against THE DECEASED and which in reality never took place. All with costs.
The defendant preliminarily objected to the inadmissibility of the plaintiff's claims on the grounds of vagueness and indeterminacy, due to the lengthy and confusing indication of property values, insufficient indication of cadastral data and the inclusion of items relating to alleged claims subsequent to the opening of the succession.
On the merits, the defendant contested word for word all of the plaintiff's allegations, providing a detailed account of the correspondence between the parties regarding the management of joint assets and the division proposals under discussion between the parties relating to alleged donations made to HEIR 3, who had confessed out of court to having received donations from his mother worth over two million euros.
The defendant also claimed that RELATIVE 1 had made multiple and significant direct and indirect donations to his wife, constituting practically the entire estate of the deceased. Therefore, these should not be taken into account for the purposes of reconstructing THE DECEASED's estate, but rather with reference to the reconstruction of her father's estate. The defendant therefore listed the assets forming part of the deceased's estate.
He also claimed to have received, together with his son RELATIVE 4, a donation from THE DECEASED of an apartment in (OMISSIS), Madonna di Campiglio, with exemption from collation specified in the deed. In addition, GRANDCHILD 1, the plaintiff's daughter, received a donation from her grandmother of an apartment in (OMISSIS). HEIR 4 received two attics located in (OMISSIS) and an apartment in Trieste from RELATIVE 1.
The defendant then objected that the deceased, having worked as a teacher for only a few years before giving up her job to devote herself to her family, had not saved anything from her modest salary and very modest pension of approximately £200.00, which she had only received after a long period of time during which she would have been without income. In particular, the flats referred to in points 1 to 17 and 10 and 11 indicated in the statement would be the result of indirect donations by her husband.
The flat in Madonna di Campiglio was donated directly by RELATIVE 1 by deed of donation dated 22 November 2001. The apartment in Via (OMISSIS) was first donated by the deceased to HEIR 3, who then returned it to the deceased's estate. All the properties and jewellery were in any case purchased with income from RELATIVE 1's work and with money belonging exclusively to him: therefore, they should be included in RELATIVE 1's estate, and to this end, the defendant made a specific request as well as a request for a reduction in direct and indirect donations due to infringement of the legitimate share.
THE DECEASED then made further donations, disguised as sales, to HEIR 3. These were, in particular, the sales transactions of 1995, 1996 and 1999 concerning the bare ownership of portions of a condominium building located in (OMISSIS), the full ownership of properties located in Forlì, via (OMISSIS) 52 with adjacent agricultural land, and the bare ownership of an apartment in (OMISSIS). In the private deed produced under doc. 33, in particular, HEIR 3 made a confession regarding the nature of these deeds as indirect gifts.
These donations, together with the other donations indicated and described by the defendant, should be subject to collation and would in any case be liable to reduction for infringement of the legitimate rights of HEIR 2. In light of the above, the defendant argued that, at the time of drafting the will, the testator could not dispose of the available portion, having already given her son HEIR 3 twice the value of the available portion through donations, thereby infringing on the defendant's legitimate portion, so that the portion actually belonging to HEIR 3 would be 1/4-.
Finally, the defendant objected that the holographic will, drawn up by THE DECEASED, was invalid. In particular, it was voidable under Article 591, paragraphs 2 and 3, of the Italian Civil Code, as it had been drawn up by the deceased in a state of natural incapacity, induced by psychological pressure. The plaintiff's assertions on this point, therefore, were completely unfounded.
Therefore, legitimate succession would apply. On this point, he objected that there were no documents confirming the validity of the will, as the necessary conditions were not met.
Finally, he objected to the unfounded nature of the plaintiff's claim of unworthiness to inherit, since the testator herself had denied any conflict with her son by including him in her will, thereby tacitly rehabilitating him. Furthermore, Article 463 of the Italian Civil Code is a rule of strict interpretation and mandatory application. The claim for revocation on the grounds of ingratitude was also completely unfounded, as it was baseless, reckless and unfounded, based on untrue and disputed circumstances, and the defendant objected to its forfeiture in light of the provision of Article 802 of the Italian Civil Code.
The defendant HEIR 2 also objected to the unfounded nature of the plaintiff's argument that the loan for use of the house in Via (OMISSIS) was attributable to an indirect donation, both in law and in fact. As for the property in Madonna di Campiglio, located in the Condominium (OMISSIS), it would generate an annual profit practically equal to zero due to the wear and tear of the assets and the constant need for minor and major repairs and maintenance; on the contrary, the defendant HEIR 2 would be entitled to reimbursement of all expenses paid for bills, utilities and condominium fees, taking into account that the apartment would always have been free and available for the mixed use of all, thus not invoking Art. 723 of the Italian Civil Code or Art. 263 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure could be invoked, as the conditions for doing so were not met.
With regard to the property in (OMISSIS), the defendant HEIR 2 denied ever having had it on loan for use; instead, with everyone's consent, it had been granted on loan for use to GRANDCHILD 2. Finally, he denied having received the indirect gifts attributed to him by the plaintiff. He contested the alleged donations made by HEIR 3 to his mother, as they concerned the return of properties already donated by the mother herself.
HEIR 3 appeared in court in a timely manner, formulating conclusions [as transcribed above].
HEIR 3, agreeing with the defence of his brother HEIR 1, stated that he had informed the other heirs of the existence of the will since the date of death and had proceeded with its publication after attempts at reaching an agreement had failed. HEIR 2's challenge to the will was therefore completely reckless, as it was entirely belated and ineffective, given that he had long been aware of the existence of the will and had ratified it in the meantime.
The will was, in any case, fully valid and effective and had been drawn up by a person in full possession of their mental faculties, as evidenced by the documents and medical records attached. The bad faith of HEIR 2 is therefore evident, as he tacitly confirmed or validated the will by executing it with substantial acquiescence to the will itself. The statements attached to the case files by the defendant HEIR 2 are also completely false.
The inheritance shares should be determined in light of the recent ruling by the Joint Divisions of the Court of Cassation, according to which the father's renunciation would increase the available share so that the defendant HEIR 3 would be entitled to 5/8 of the maternal estate, or, alternatively, the share of V2 of the estate, or 7/16 according to the classic criterion also followed by the Notary.
The defendant HEIR 3 then listed the assets forming part of the relictum, as indicated in the declaration of succession. The properties located in (OMISSIS), registered in the name of HEIR 4, would also belong to the estate, as they were purchased with money from THE DECEASED obtained from the sale of an apartment in (OMISSIS). In addition, HEIR 3 had made two property donations to his mother, the value of which should be counted in favour of HEIR 3.
As for securities and money, they were divided by agreement between the parties into equal shares of €200,000.00 each.
HEIR 2 would be obliged to report on the two properties in Bologna and Madonna di Campiglio, which he managed alone without allowing his other siblings to use them, and the defendant would be obliged to give the other heirs their respective shares of the income generated by the properties. Furthermore, there would be no evidence that HEIR 2, regarding improvements to the flats in Via (OMISSIS). With regard to the loan for use enjoyed by HEIR 2, he agreed with the plaintiff's position, as well as on the non-collatability or reducibility of donations made to third parties who were not heirs.
The request for reduction made by HEIR 2 would also be completely inadmissible due to failure to accept with the benefit of inventory and failure to specify the necessary constituent elements.
With regard to the properties sold by the deceased to the defendant HEIR 3, the latter objected to the limitation period for the action for simulation. He then proceeded to list the donations and gifts received by himself and the other heirs of the deceased, finally proposing various division scenarios.
In the event of even partial acceptance of HEIR 2's claims, the defendant HEIR 3 invoked the paternal indemnity/guarantee of €250,000.00 to his advantage.
On the request for revocation of the donations to HEIR 2 on grounds of ingratitude, he agreed with the plaintiff's arguments.
Finally, HEIR 4 appeared in court in a timely manner, formulating conclusions [as transcribed above].
The defendant HEIR 4 agreed with the plaintiff's defence regarding the validity of the deceased's will.
On the distribution of shares, the defendant agreed with the notary's proposal, i.e. 7/16 to HEIR 3 and 3/16 to the others. He then proceeded to list the assets forming part of the estate.
He agreed with HEIR 1's argument regarding HEIR 2's sole management of the property in Madonna di Campiglio and Via (OMISSIS). He also agreed with the plaintiff's position on the loan for use of Via (OMISSIS). He again objected to the non-reducibility of donations made to third parties. He then listed the assets to be attributed to the estate for collation, requesting their division.
It should be noted that the present case essentially concerns: i) the determination of the composition of the estate of the deceased THE DECEASED, ii) the determination of the nature of the inheritance, whether testamentary or legitimate, iii) the identification of the heirs and the nature and extent of their respective shares, iv) the handling of requests for reduction/collation/revocation of donations relating to assets belonging to the estate of THE DECEASED, v) the consequent division of the estate of THE DECEASED.
On the contrary, the counterclaims of HEIR 2 concerning the estate of RELATIVE 1 must be considered and declared inadmissible, as they are not relevant to the present proceedings, since they concern separate estates, especially since neither spouse was, in fact, the heir of the other, the former having renounced his inheritance (see doc. 22 in the plaintiff's file), the second because she predeceased him.
Therefore, the following counterclaims by HEIR 2 must be declared inadmissible:

to revoke, on the grounds of ingratitude pursuant to Article 801 of the Italian Civil Code, the direct and indirect donations and atypical gifts made by RELATIVE 1 to HEIR 1 and HEIR 3;
to ascertain the value of the estate of RELATIVE 1 to the extent indicated in the narrative of the writ of summons introducing the proceedings RG 3958/17;
ascertain and declare the reserved portion of the aforementioned estates of the deceased to which HEIR 2 is entitled, to the extent indicated in the narrative of the writ of summons introducing the proceedings RG 3958/17 or to the extent that may emerge during the proceedings, and consequently, reduce, pursuant to Articles 553 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code, the portions of the legitimate heirs and/or testamentary dispositions and/or direct and/or indirect and/or concealed donations and/or atypical gifts (with reference to the succession of RELATIVE 1);
order the division pursuant to Article 713 of the Italian Civil Code among the co-heirs of the deceased lawyer RELATIVE 1;
order the collation pursuant to Article 737 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code of direct and/or indirect and/or concealed donations and/or atypical gifts in favour of the co-heirs HEIR 1 and HEIR 3 (with reference to the deceased RELATIVE 1);
in any case, order the collation pursuant to Article 737 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code of direct and/or indirect and/or atypical donations in favour of the co-heir HEIR 4 (with reference to the deceased RELATIVE 1);
declare that HEIR 1 and HEIR 3 have forfeited the benefit of inventory with respect to the inheritance of RELATIVE 1, with all legal consequences.

That said, the request to join case no. 3958/17 RG to the present case must once again be rejected, as the conditions for doing so do not exist, since, as we have seen, these are two separate successions.
HEIR 2's objection regarding the alleged inadmissibility due to the vagueness of the writ of summons must also be rejected, since the points of contention between the parties appear clear and evident and the adversarial proceedings seem to have been exhaustively explained on all points of dispute.
At this point, it is necessary to question the nature of THE DECEASED's inheritance, whether testamentary or legitimate. In this regard, as regards the request for annulment of the will of 17 June 2007, HEIR 2 did not reproduce this request in the clarification of the conclusions, stating instead that he no longer had any interest in pursuing it.
In particular, HEIR 2 writes in his reply brief: 'It is reiterated that the writer has brought a legally founded and admissible action on the grounds of the invalidity of what turned out to be the second will published prior to the previous one dated 6 September 2006 but published only on 11 September 2018. It is clear that HEIR 2 no longer has an interest in pursuing the application for annulment of the subsequent will of THE DECEASED dated 17 June 2007. In fact, even if the action for annulment of THE DECEASED's will of 17 June 2007 were to be upheld, the mortis causa provision of the previous will would remain, which establishes the four children as heirs to the legitimate portion, leaving the disposable portion to the son HEIR 3. More precisely, the declaration of annulment of the second will would not benefit the writer, HEIR 2, given that the previous will, which was concealed in bad faith by HEIR 3 for many years, would be taken into consideration. The refusal to declare the second will valid would still not change the situation, given that the tacit revocation of the will occurs when the provisions of the subsequent will are incompatible with the previous one, in accordance with Article 682 of the Italian Civil Code, a scenario that would not occur in this case, since THE DECEASED named her four children as heirs to the legitimate portion in both wills, leaving the disposable portion to her son HEIR 3'.
On the procedural outcome of this claim, the case law of the Court of Cassation has highlighted that 'The cessation of the matter in dispute - which may well be declared in the Court of Cassation - presupposes the settlement of the dispute and the loss, due to a supervening event or fact, of any interest of the parties in continuing the proceedings. The situation thus created, in which all grounds for dispute have been completely removed, must be clearly recognised and accepted by all parties concerned, unless the action has been waived in substance, with the consequent radical elimination of the dispute" (Cass. Sez. L, Judgment No. 576 of 21/01/1994).
In the present case, it is clear that the action has been waived in substance, as expressly stated by HEIR 2, and that this waiver must be ascertained and declared, while there are no grounds for the termination of the matter in dispute. In any case, the costs will be settled in the final decision.
Therefore, given that the validity of the will is no longer in question, it must be ascertained and declared that the succession of THE DECEASED, who died in (OMISSIS), was opened by virtue of the holographic will dated 17 June 2007 and published on 11 January 2013 by the Notary THIRD PARTY 2 of Forlì (doc. 19, 21 plaintiff's file).
The contents of the will are as follows: "I, THE DECEASED, born in Dovadola (Forlì) on 20 February 1927, being of sound mind, hereby dispose of my assets for the time when I am no longer alive: I appoint my children HEIR 4, HEIR 1, HEIR 2 and HEIR 3 as my heirs. I assign to my son HEIR 3 my available share in addition to the reserve to which he is entitled. Forlì, 17 June 2007."
As regards the determination of the identity of the heirs, it seems clear that they are the children of THE DECEASED, given that her husband, who was still alive at the time, is not even mentioned in the will and, in any case, as we have seen, he renounced his wife's inheritance.
However, the plaintiff is bringing a claim against HEIR 2 under Article 463 of the Italian Civil Code for exclusion from succession on grounds of unworthiness. As is well known and emphasised by case law, the cases of unworthiness to inherit provided for in the aforementioned provision are exhaustive and cannot be interpreted broadly or analogously (see Court of Palermo, Section II, 22/02/2019, Court of Trieste, 13/03/2019, (hearing 07/03/2019, filed 13/03/2019), no. 137, DeJure).
The plaintiff therefore specifies that the formulation of the claim of unworthiness is subject to the acceptance of the objection of constitutional illegitimacy and/or the request for a preliminary ruling on the provision, insofar as it does not provide, as grounds for exclusion from succession, the behaviour of the subject/co-heir, not prior to but subsequent to the death of the deceased, aimed at preventing the actual fulfilment of the deceased's wishes, by delaying the publication of the will with threats and cajoling and then contesting the will itself despite having confirme; Third Part of full text: deceased's estate, respectively, in accordance with the provisions of Article 537, paragraphs 1 and 2, of the Italian Civil Code. With reference to the case provided for in Article 542, paragraph 1, of the Italian Civil Code, the question arises as to whether the failure of the only child to exercise the right of reduction results in the expansion of the spouse's legitimate share, so that it reaches the amount provided for in Article 540, paragraph 1, of the Italian Civil Code. Finally, with reference to the case provided for in Article 542, paragraph 2, of the Italian Civil Code, the question arises as to whether the exercise of the action for reduction by only one of the children means that the legitimate portion to which he or she is entitled must be determined in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 1.
The case law of this Supreme Court has been favourable to the thesis of the so-called expansion of the reserved portion with reference to the case of failure to bring an action for reduction by the surviving spouse (judgments no. 3888 of 26 October 1976; 9 March 1987, no. 2434; 11 February 1995, no. 1529). In this regard, it has been stated (judgment no. 2434 of 9 March 1987, cited above) that... it must be borne in mind that, pursuant to Article 521 of the Italian Civil Code, the renunciation of inheritance is retroactive in the sense that the renouncing heir is considered as if he or she had never been called to inherit. It is therefore impossible to refer to the situation existing at the time of the opening of the succession, since that situation is subject to change, as a result of any renunciations, with retroactive effect. It is therefore necessary to refer to the actual situation, and not to the theoretical one, referring to the moment of the opening of the succession, regardless of the events that occurred subsequently; reference must therefore be made to the heirs who actually participate in the distribution of the estate and not to those who, in theory, could have participated in such distribution.
This approach is consistent with legal doctrine, which also invokes the principle of retroactivity of renunciation established in Article 521 of the Civil Code and argues that an argument in favour of this principle can be inferred from Article 538 of the Civil Code, which regulates the reserve due to ascendants 'if the deceased leaves no legitimate children', as the rule should only apply if the deceased had no children or if they are all present or absent; if, on the other hand, there are surviving children capable of inheriting and they all renounce their inheritance, it should be concluded that either the reserved share of two-thirds established by Article 537 of the Italian Civil Code remains in favour of the ascendants, or that no right of reserve arises in favour of the ascendants, both conclusions being clearly inadmissible. This is an approach that the panel does not agree with.
Firstly, it seems inappropriate to refer to the effects of the renunciation of one of the heirs in matters of legitimate succession, as provided for in Articles 521 and 522 of the Civil Code, for various reasons.
In legitimate succession, the so-called retroactive effect of the renunciation of one of the beneficiaries and the consequent increase in favour of the acceptors finds a logical explanation in the fact that, otherwise, it would not be known what would happen to the share of the renouncing party.
The situation is quite different with regard to so-called compulsory succession.
The legislator has taken care to ensure that each of the legitimate heirs is guaranteed a portion of the deceased's estate, even against the latter's wishes. In the absence of a joint call to a share considered globally with reference to the hypothesis of multiple beneficiaries (and indeed, since the lack of a hereditary call is the basis of compulsory succession), on the one hand, the logical assumption of a theoretical increase falls away, and, on the other hand, there is no uncertainty as to the fate of the share (in theory) due to the legitimate heir who does not exercise the right of reduction: the donees or heirs or legatees, in fact, retain a portion of the deceased's assets greater than that which the latter could have disposed of.
The letter of the law, moreover, constitutes an insurmountable obstacle to adherence to the thesis hitherto upheld in doctrine and jurisprudence. From the wording of Article 537 of the Civil Code, paragraph 1 ("if the parent leaves"), Article 538 of the Civil Code, paragraph 1 ("if the deceased does not leave"), Article 542 of the Civil Code, paragraph 1 ("if the deceased leaves"), 542 of the Italian Civil Code, paragraph 2 ("when the deceased leaves"), it is clear that, for the purposes of calculating the reserved portion, reference must be made to the situation existing at the time of the opening of the succession; on the other hand, the bringing of an action for reduction by only some of the legitimate heirs is not taken into consideration for this purpose. Therefore, the essential conditions (the existence of a gap to be filled and the possibility of applying the principle of ubi eadem ratio ibi eadem legis dispositio) for an analogous extension of the rules on legitimate succession are lacking. The criticised thesis also seems to conflict with the rationale behind compulsory succession, which is not only to guarantee certain relatives a portion of the deceased's estate, but also (on the flip side) to allow the deceased to know within what limits, considering the composition of their family, they can dispose of their estate in favour of third parties. It is clear that the need for certainty in question would not be satisfied if this share were to be determined, after the opening of the succession, on the basis of the number of legitimate heirs who might bring an action for reduction. Furthermore, the practical drawbacks associated with the so-called expansion of the reserved share cannot be ignored.
To this end, it is necessary to start from the consideration that the exercise of the action for reduction is subject to the ordinary ten-year limitation period and that there is no provision for an actio interrogatoria, unlike what happens with regard to the acceptance of inheritance (Article 481 of the Italian Civil Code). It follows that, at the opening of the succession, each legitimate heir may bring an action for reduction only with regard to the portion of the deceased's estate to which he or she would be entitled on the basis of the latter's family situation at that time. Only after the other legitimate heirs have waived their right to bring an action for reduction or after the limitation period has expired to their detriment may he or she take action to obtain a supplement to the legitimate portion, with obvious uncertainty in the meantime as to the fate of a portion of the assets that the deceased has disposed of by donation or will in favour of third parties.
Nor can any useful arguments in favour of the criticised thesis be inferred from Article 538 of the Civil Code. Firstly, in the reasoning transcribed above, the reference to a two-thirds share reserved for ascendants by Article 537 of the Civil Code is incomprehensible, since that provision refers to the share reserved for legitimate or natural children.
Furthermore, it is not clear why the conclusion (which would be reached by adhering to the argument that the court considers preferable) that, if the deceased's legitimate children survive and all renounce their inheritance, no right of legitimate inheritance would arise in favour of the ascendants, would be inadmissible. First of all, it should be noted that it is not clear whether the renunciation refers to the acceptance of the inheritance or to the bringing of an action for reduction.
In the first case, the issue of protecting ascendants would not even arise, as the legitimate succession pursuant to Article 569 of the Italian Civil Code would apply in their favour, since the legitimate children, having renounced their inheritance, would be considered as never having been called to succession.
In the second case, the exclusion of the possibility of a reserved share in favour of ascendants would be an expression of the legislator's choice to guarantee the acquisition of a share of the deceased's estate only to the closest relatives (as well as the spouse) existing at the time of the opening of the succession. Relatives of a subsequent degree, who are considered legitimate only in the absence of those of a closer degree, therefore, cannot be reinstated in the event of failure by the latter to exercise the right of reduction. Ultimately, the legislator considered it unfair for the deceased to dispose of his entire estate in favour of strangers if he had only descendants or only ascendants; However, it did not consider it unfair that the acts by which the deceased, who leaves descendants and ascendants, disposed of his entire estate in favour of strangers remain valid if the descendants (the only legitimate heirs considered) do not exercise the right of reduction.
In light of the above considerations, it can therefore be concluded that, for the purposes of determining the reserved portion due to the individual categories of legitimate heirs and to the individual legitimate heirs within the same category, reference must be made to the situation existing at the time of the opening of the succession and not to that which arises as a result of the failure (due to renunciation or prescription) of any of the legitimate heirs to bring an action for reduction'.
In doctrine, however, it has been noted that the above-mentioned orientation of the SSUU would apply only to cases of renunciation or prescription of the action for reduction, not to renunciation of inheritance, as in the present case (doc. 22 plaintiff's file), and this by emphasising Article 552 of the Civil Code as the key provision, which states: 'The legitimate heir (Articles 536 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code) who renounces the inheritance (Article 519 of the Italian Civil Code), when there is no representation (Article 467 of the Italian Civil Code), may retain the donations (Articles 769 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code) or obtain the legacies made to him (Article 521 of the Italian Civil Code) from the available portion; but when there has been no express waiver of imputation (Articles 553, 564 and 724 of the Italian Civil Code), if it is necessary to reduce (Article 553 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code) the testamentary dispositions or donations (Article 554 of the Italian Civil Code) in order to supplement the legitimate portion due to the heirs, the allocations made by the testator on the disposable portion, which would not be subject to reduction if the legitimate heir accepted the inheritance, remain unaffected, and the donations and legacies made to the latter are reduced"; in the Report of the Minister of Justice G.D. to the Civil Code of 4 April 1942, we read:
"One issue that I have re-examined is that of the fate of donations and legacies on account of the legitimate portion in the event of renunciation by the beneficiary. As is well known, the 1865 code provided in this regard that the renouncing party may retain the donation or claim the legacy up to the amount of the disposable portion, while he or she may not retain or obtain anything by way of legitimate portion. The provision, reproduced verbatim in Article 338 of the preliminary draft, was deleted in the final draft because it was considered superfluous, since in the new system, those who do not accept are not heirs, and only heirs are required to collate and are entitled to the legitimate portion. The accuracy of this principle with regard to the right to the legitimate portion has not been disputed. However, the opinion has been expressed that it would be preferable to reinstate the provision relating to the exemption from collation by the renouncing party, in order to avoid any doubt that he or she may retain the donation or claim the legacy even beyond the limit of the available portion. This proposal led me to re-examine the advisability of overcoming the traditional solution to the problem, which has been almost unanimously criticised by legal scholars. It has indeed been observed that the practical consequences of applying the provision of Article 1003 of the old code are often contrary to the foresight and wishes of the head of the family who has made assignments in anticipation of inheritance. In fact, the renunciation of succession by a child who has benefited from a donation on account of the legitimate portion increases the legitimate portion of the other children and may therefore result in a reduction in the gifts made by the deceased as disposable assets, which would not have been subject to reduction if the legitimate heir had accepted. I recognised these observations as fully justified and therefore considered it necessary to seek a different solution that would reconcile the following fundamental principles: a) respect for the wishes of the deceased, who, by making the donation on account of the legitimate portion, did not intend to preclude the possibility of allocating the disposable portion as he wished or to alter the situation of the other legitimate heirs; b) the principle that the renouncing party should not receive anything by way of legitimate portion; c) the principle that, since the renouncing party is considered extraneous to the inheritance, the other legitimate heirs must absorb the entire legitimate portion; d) the requirement that any beneficiaries of the disposable portion should not be at the mercy of the renouncing party. One possible system would have been to charge donations or legacies on account of the legitimate portion to the unavailable portion; but this system seemed incongruous to me, because it would have given the renouncing party an excessively advantageous position. In fact, the renouncing party could have retained the legitimate portion and the surplus on the disposable portion, whereas according to the rule of the 1865 code, they cannot retain anything as a legitimate portion. Another system I considered was to provide for the cancellation of any donation or bequest on account of the legitimate portion for the part corresponding to the legitimate portion; but I had to reject this solution as well because it would have the disadvantage of rescinding acts of generosity made within the family after some time, contrary to the presumed will of the disposer. I therefore decided to adopt a fourth system, according to which the renouncing heir may retain the donations or obtain the legacies made to him, on the disposable portion, provided that this does not prejudice the allocations made by the testator on the disposable portion that would not have been subject to reduction if the heir had come into the succession. Therefore, if it is necessary to reduce testamentary dispositions or gifts in order to supplement the legitimate portion due to the heirs, the allocations made by the deceased on the available portion, which would not have been affected if the renouncing heir had come into the succession, remain unaffected; on the other hand, the following are reduced donations and bequests made to the renouncing party. In essence, the order in which the action for reduction must be brought by the accepting heirs is changed, who must take action against the renouncing party, respecting the other allocations on the available estate. The fairness of this solution, which takes due account of the various requirements I mentioned above, does not seem to me to be questionable. According to this argument, the provision in question would therefore mean that, in the event of renunciation of the inheritance by the legitimate heir, the reserved shares of the other legitimate heirs would have to be recalculated, while the theory of the so-called 'crystallisation' of shares should be limited to cases of renunciation or prescription of the action for reduction.
In fact, in case law on the merits, applications of the principle of 'crystallisation' can also be found in cases of renunciation of inheritance (cf. Vicenza Court, 28/10/2021, no. 1976, DeJure); another court of first instance points out, in particular, that the renunciation of inheritance by the pretermitted heir would be without effect since the inheritance had not been opened in his favour: in particular, "... in the absence of a successful action for reduction, the renunciation by the pretermitted heir is without effect, as there is no share of the inheritance that remains unacquired as a result of the renunciation itself, given that in the case of a pretermitted heir, there is no inheritance in his favour. (r.g.a.c. no. 3491/2011, 3492/2011, 6156/2012). Therefore, in order to acquire the share due to the pretermitted heir, it is necessary to first successfully challenge the waiver of the action for reduction, which eliminates the effectiveness of the testamentary provisions that are detrimental to the rights of the pretermitted heir (...) Although the Court appears to have dealt only with the consequences of waiving the right to bring an action for reduction, there is no doubt that the same practical result can be achieved even in the case of renunciation of inheritance. Where, in fact, the person to whom the law reserves a share of the inheritance has only been prejudiced, by renouncing the (partial) inheritance in his favour, provided that the conditions for representation in favour of the descendants of the person renouncing the inheritance do not apply in relation to the amount of inheritance devolving to him by will or by legitimate succession, he will lose all inheritance rights and will also be precluded from bringing an action for reduction. r.g.a.c. no. 3491/2011, 3492/2011, 6156/2012 Similarly, the pretermitted heir, excluded from the inheritance, by renouncing the right to take legal action to reduce the prejudicial provisions, will no longer be able to obtain the share reserved for him by law and will lose the only possibility of claiming the inheritance of the deceased. In one way or another, the legitimate heir will not be included in the succession. Ultimately, the interpretation of the Supreme Court, in its enlarged composition, certainly has the merit of simplifying the calculation of the reserved share due to the legitimate heir, which becomes insensitive to subsequent events. The Court therefore considers it necessary to reiterate that if the deceased leaves a number of legitimate heirs who are harmed by donations or testamentary dispositions that exceed the available share, the failure of one of them to bring an action for reduction does not affect the share due to the others and does not increase it. Instead, it is the donee, heir or legatee who are the recipients of the detrimental provision, to benefit from the choice of the renouncing or inactive heir, in that, for the relevant share, they may retain the attribution in their favour. There is no reason to depart from this principle, given its consistency with the letter and purpose of the provisions..." (Court of Palermo, Section II, 17/07/2017, No. 3952; DeJure). Therefore, it must be considered that even in the case of renunciation of inheritance, it is not possible to deviate from the ruling of the SSSUU, given that the practical effect and the protection requirements underlying this case are similar to the case explicitly addressed by the Court.
These principles must then be coordinated with the testamentary nature of the inheritance in the case in question and with the need to respect the wishes of the deceased, as mentioned above. It is reiterated that the will reads as follows: 'I, the undersigned THE DECEASED, born in (OMISSIS), in full possession of my mental faculties, hereby dispose of my assets for the time when I am no longer alive: I appoint my children HEIR 4, HEIR 1, HEIR 2 and HEIR 3 as my heirs. I assign to my son HEIR 3 my disposable portion in addition to the reserve to which he is entitled. Forlì, 17 June 2007". The reserve due to all the children must be calculated in accordance with Article 542, paragraph 2, of the Italian Civil Code, by virtue of the aforementioned principle of crystallisation, since the deceased, at the time of her death, 'left' a husband and four children. The legitimate share of the latter is unaffected by subsequent events, so that RELATIVE 1's renunciation cannot determine the increase (hypothesis 1) or recalculation (hypothesis 3) of the shares of the children to whom THE DECEASED clearly intended to leave only the reserved share. The ideal share due to RELATIVE 1 can only be attributed to the available portion for a total of 4/8 (2/8 + 2/8 RELATIVE 1 share); therefore, the shares must be recalculated as follows: HEIR 2 1/8, HEIR 1 1/8, HEIR 4 1/8, HEIR 3 5/8 (equal to 1/8 + 2/8 + 2/8).
Finally, the following requests by HEIR 2 must be declared inadmissible, as they are new and were only proposed late in the clarification of the conclusions:
"ASSURE AND DECLARE that HEIR 3 violated Article 620 of the Italian Civil Code with regard to the failure to submit the holographic will to the notary for publication as soon as news of the testator's death was received, having concealed the holographic will of 6 September 2006 of the deceased THE DECEASED, who was already ill at the time but certainly capable of understanding and willing, a will published on 11 September 2018 by the notary THIRD PARTY 3 of Forlì; ASSURE AND DECLARE that the aforementioned HEIR 3 violated all duties of loyalty and integrity by publishing the holographic will of THE DECEASED dated 17 June 2007 late in 2013, concealing, on that occasion, the will dated 6 September 2006 and creating the conditions for the challenge - proposed by writ of summons for civil case no. 3958/17 r.g., relating to the division of the estates of RELATIVE 1 and THE DECEASED - given the incapacity to make a will of the aforementioned THE DECEASED two months before her death; for failing, in the face of the challenge to the aforementioned holographic will of 17 June 2007, to inform the judge and the undersigned plaintiff challenging the aforementioned will of 17 June 2007 of the existence of another will - of which the other two co-heirs were also aware, certainly HEIR 1, who was the first to produce it by filing it pursuant to Article 87 of the implementing provisions dated 6 September 2006, thereby causing the judge and the co-heir to mistakenly believe that the will of 17 June 2007 was the only will, acting in absolute bad faith and in violation of every duty of loyalty and integrity in hearing the case with regard to the will of 17 June 2007 - considering it more favourable to him than the will of 6 September 2006 - so that the investigating judge admitted evidence for formal questioning and for witnesses with regard to the mental condition of THE DECEASED on 17 June 2007".
With regard to the following questions from HEIR 2: "ASSURE AND DECLARE that the production of the holographic will of 6 September 2006 - null and void and ineffective for the reasons already expressed regarding the complete disposal of his estate by THE DECEASED, who was otherwise capable in September 2006 - in the course of the present case 3958/17 r.g. by means of a reconventio reconventionis is procedural conduct punishable on the basis of the case law of the Supreme Court, ex plurimis Cass. Civ., 12.09.2003, no. 13427, which states: "Pursuant to Article 92, paragraph 1, of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, the violation of the duty of loyalty and probity established by Article 88 of the aforementioned code justifies, regardless of the outcome of the case, the condemnation of the party that has failed to fulfil this duty to reimburse the legal costs that the other party has had to incur as a result of the unlawful conduct. Therefore, the judge does not violate the principle of liability for costs by ordering the winning party to pay the costs of the proceedings, where he or she finds - with discretionary assessment that cannot be reviewed on grounds of legitimacy, if adequately justified in relation to the logic and reality of the proceedings - that this was made necessary by the conduct of the winning party in violation of the aforementioned duty"; ASSURED that HEIR 1's involvement in the aforementioned conduct in violation of Article 88 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure is manifestly in bad faith, for having even filed a copy of the aforementioned will on 6 September 2006 after appearing in court with an irregular filing, these, being relevant to the costs of the proceedings, will be settled at the final stage.
That being established, the case must be remanded for the continuation of the preliminary investigation into the other claims.
Costs to be settled at the final stage.

FACTUAL AND LEGAL GROUNDS (CONCISE STATEMENT)
HEIR 1 (hereinafter also referred to as 'the plaintiff' or 'HEIR 1') brought legal proceedings against HEIR 2 (hereinafter also referred to as 'HEIR 2'), HEIR 3 (hereinafter also referred to as 'HEIR 3'), HEIR 4 (hereinafter also referred to as "HEIR 4"), and THIRD PARTY 1 (hereinafter also referred to as "THIRD PARTY 1") (collectively referred to as "the defendants") to ascertain and declare HEIR 2's unworthiness to inherit, with an order for the immediate return of all assets and proceeds from the opening of the succession; to uphold the action pursuant to Article 801 of the Italian Civil Code against HEIR 2 for the serious, intolerable and repeated abuse of his mother THE DECEASED as described in the narrative, with the aforementioned defendant being ordered to return to the estate all donations received from his mother during her lifetime, as detailed in the documents; to declare the full validity of the holographic will drawn up by THE DECEASED on 17 June 2017 and subsequently published by the Notary THIRD PARTY 2 of Forlì, as it was drawn up by a person of sound mind, declaring the challenge to the will by HEIR 2 in the settlement agreement of 28 April 2017, ordering HEIR 2 to compensate the plaintiff for all damages for the serious offences directed at the mother, father and the plaintiff himself in the same deed, settling said compensation in the amount of €40,000 or any other higher or lower sum deemed fair pursuant to Article 1226 of the Italian Civil Code; to order HEIR 2 to pay the sum of €100,000.00 or such other sum as may be deemed fair for the sole management of the properties in Via (OMISSIS); to order HEIR 2 to provide an account pursuant to Article 263 of the Italian Civil Code of the rents and utilities received in respect of the two rents highlighted; to ascertain the nature of indirect generosity, for the sum of €144,000.00 or such other sum as may be deemed fair, of the loan for use of the property located at Via (OMISSIS) granted by the mother to her son HEIR 2 for the purposes of fictitious reunification; for the dissolution of the joint ownership of the inheritance with the attribution to the plaintiff of the assets corresponding to his ideal share of co-ownership (equal to 3/16). All with costs.
The plaintiff stated that his mother, THE DECEASED, died on 20 August 2007. In her youth, Ms THE DECEASED had obtained a degree in French language and literature; During the 1950s, she taught in various schools and high schools for about ten years, until she made an agreement with her husband, RELATIVE 1, whereby, in exchange for her wife giving up her teaching career and her contribution to the family and children, as well as the management of family affairs, she would receive various financial payments from her husband.
The marriage produced four children, HEIR 3, HEIR 1, HEIR 4 and HEIR 2, who are the current parties to the case. The marital union continued over time until, in 2005-2006, Mrs THE DECEASED learned that she was suffering from a serious illness, which led to her death after years of surgery and treatment. Until her death, despite her suffering, the deceased remained lucid, although her ability to speak had diminished in recent times.
The deceased left a holographic will, dated 17 June 2007, in which she named her children HEIR 3, HEIR 1, HEIR 4 and HEIR 2 as heirs, assigning to the latter, in addition to the reserved portion, her own disposable portion. The other heirs were immediately informed of the existence of the will by HEIR 3, who, however, waited to publish it, at the request of HEIR 2, pending a settlement of the disputes between the siblings, which never came. Thus, the will was published on 11 January 2013 by Notary THIRD PARTY 2.
The plaintiff pointed out that the defendant HEIR 2 had never contested the will, but had instead given it his full confirmation.
Subsequently, on 26 December 2016, the father and husband of the deceased, RELATIVE 1, also died. Only after the death of the father, on 5 January 2017, did the defendant HEIR 2 express his intention to contest the will of THE DECEASED, claiming that it was voidable.
However, in the plaintiff's opinion, the will was fully valid, as the deceased was fully lucid and aware at the time of drafting the will, given that the deceased's lucidity never waned, despite her illness, and only declined from August 2007, i.e. two months after the will was drafted and shortly before her death. The deceased also attended a party for her daughter-in-law RELATIVE 2's birthday on 28 July 2007, where she sang and conversed with the other guests. The text of the will is clear and unambiguous, as well as logical and conclusive in its content.
The defendant HEIR 2's challenge to the will is completely reckless and likely to result in liability for damages, given the obvious harm caused to his mother, father and brother. The husband and father of the parties, RELATIVE 1, having seen the will, in which he did not appear, renounced his inheritance, thus confirming the validity of the will itself.
Moreover, the deceased's wish to benefit her son HEIR 3 was linked to profound reasons well known to the parties, and the contestation of the will would in any case be covered by the five-year statute of limitations. Finally, there were multiple acts by HEIR 2 confirming recognition of the will and the shares arising from it, as specified in the deeds.
The plaintiff also argued that the defendant HEIR 2 was unworthy of succession; in particular, the act of contesting the will constituted a manifestation of genuine aversion towards his mother, with whom he had always had a conflictual relationship, partly due to a radically different outlook on life. The defendant HEIR 2 had also put forward the absurd and offensive argument that his mother was merely a fictitious owner of her husband's assets, without money or rights, incapable of saving and lacking technical and legal knowledge, all circumstances far from reality, and had also falsely claimed that his mother was incapable of understanding and willing at the time of the will.
In reality, the deceased had left teaching only because of an agreement reached with her husband, which had nothing to do with the donation, but fell within the scope of Article 2034 of the Italian Civil Code, and had therefore devoted herself to caring for her family and also to managing her husband's affairs, in particular his real estate assets. In any case, Ms THE DECEASED also owned her own assets, independently of her husband, jointly with her brothers THIRD PARTY 1 and RELATIVE 3.
That said, the plaintiff expressed his intention to raise 1) a question of constitutional legitimacy and 2) a preliminary ruling on the acts to the EU in relation to Article 463 of the Civil Code.
In particular, in relation to Article 3 of the Constitution, Article 463 of the Civil Code would be unconstitutional insofar as it does not provide for any cause for exclusion from succession the behaviour of the heir prior to or after the death of the deceased, aimed at preventing the fulfilment of the deceased's last wishes, in particular by attempting to delay the publication of the will, through threats and cajoling, and then attempting to contest its validity despite being aware of the perfect legitimacy of the will itself. Furthermore, the legislation would also conflict with the provisions of the EU Treaty and the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.
These requests are aimed at declaring the defendant HEIR 2 unworthy of inheriting from his mother THE DECEASED.
In the alternative, the conditions for revocation on grounds of ingratitude pursuant to Article 801 of the Italian Civil Code of the donations received by HEIR 2 would exist, due to blatant disrespect, contempt, aversion and lack of gratitude towards his mother, all as manifested by the actions described above. The plaintiff then specified in the documents the donations that should be subject to revocation. The conduct of the defendant HEIR 2 would also give rise to liability for damages on his part.
The plaintiff also claimed that, after the death of the deceased, HEIR 2 had managed two apartments, located in Bologna and Madonna di Campiglio, on his own, for which he should be held accountable. In particular, he had held the property in Madonna di Campiglio for about nine years, from winter 2007 to winter/spring 2016, excluding the other siblings. There was never any loan for use of the property in question, as the siblings never had the keys, which were handed over to HEIR 2 by RELATIVE 1 himself, and the other siblings waited in vain for the management account without ever obtaining their share of the related proceeds, which were due to the plaintiff in the amount of 3/16, plus additional damages and interest.
