The case law of this Supreme Court has been favourable to the thesis of the so-called expansion of the reserved portion with reference to the case of failure to bring an action for reduction by the surviving spouse (judgments no. 3888 of 26 October 1976; 9 March 1987, no. 2434; 11 February 1995, no. 1529). In this regard, it has been stated (judgment no. 2434 of 9 March 1987, cited above) that... it must be borne in mind that, pursuant to Article 521 of the Italian Civil Code, the renunciation of inheritance is retroactive in the sense that the renouncing heir is considered as if he or she had never been called to inherit. It is therefore impossible to refer to the situation existing at the time of the opening of the succession, since that situation is subject to change, as a result of any renunciations, with retroactive effect. It is therefore necessary to refer to the actual situation, and not to the theoretical one, referring to the moment of the opening of the succession, regardless of the events that occurred subsequently; reference must therefore be made to the heirs who actually participate in the distribution of the estate and not to those who, in theory, could have participated in such distribution.
This approach is consistent with legal doctrine, which also invokes the principle of retroactivity of renunciation established in Article 521 of the Civil Code and argues that an argument in favour of this principle can be inferred from Article 538 of the Civil Code, which regulates the reserve due to ascendants 'if the deceased leaves no legitimate children', as the rule should only apply if the deceased had no children or if they are all present or absent; if, on the other hand, there are surviving children capable of inheriting and they all renounce their inheritance, it should be concluded that either the reserved share of two-thirds established by Article 537 of the Italian Civil Code remains in favour of the ascendants, or that no right of reserve arises in favour of the ascendants, both conclusions being clearly inadmissible. This is an approach that the panel does not agree with.
Firstly, it seems inappropriate to refer to the effects of the renunciation of one of the heirs in matters of legitimate succession, as provided for in Articles 521 and 522 of the Civil Code, for various reasons.
In legitimate succession, the so-called retroactive effect of the renunciation of one of the beneficiaries and the consequent increase in favour of the acceptors finds a logical explanation in the fact that, otherwise, it would not be known what would happen to the share of the renouncing party.
The situation is quite different with regard to so-called compulsory succession.
The legislator has taken care to ensure that each of the legitimate heirs is guaranteed a portion of the deceased's estate, even against the latter's wishes. In the absence of a joint call to a share considered globally with reference to the hypothesis of multiple beneficiaries (and indeed, since the lack of a hereditary call is the basis of compulsory succession), on the one hand, the logical assumption of a theoretical increase falls away, and, on the other hand, there is no uncertainty as to the fate of the share (in theory) due to the legitimate heir who does not exercise the right of reduction: the donees or heirs or legatees, in fact, retain a portion of the deceased's assets greater than that which the latter could have disposed of.
The letter of the law, moreover, constitutes an insurmountable obstacle to adherence to the thesis hitherto upheld in doctrine and jurisprudence. From the wording of Article 537 of the Civil Code, paragraph 1 ("if the parent leaves"), Article 538 of the Civil Code, paragraph 1 ("if the deceased does not leave"), Article 542 of the Civil Code, paragraph 1 ("if the deceased leaves"), 542 of the Italian Civil Code, paragraph 2 ("when the deceased leaves"), it is clear that, for the purposes of calculating the reserved portion, reference must be made to the situation existing at the time of the opening of the succession; on the other hand, the bringing of an action for reduction by only some of the legitimate heirs is not taken into consideration for this purpose. Therefore, the essential conditions (the existence of a gap to be filled and the possibility of applying the principle of ubi eadem ratio ibi eadem legis dispositio) for an analogous extension of the rules on legitimate succession are lacking. The criticised thesis also seems to conflict with the rationale behind compulsory succession, which is not only to guarantee certain relatives a portion of the deceased's estate, but also (on the flip side) to allow the deceased to know within what limits, considering the composition of their family, they can dispose of their estate in favour of third parties. It is clear that the need for certainty in question would not be satisfied if this share were to be determined, after the opening of the succession, on the basis of the number of legitimate heirs who might bring an action for reduction. Furthermore, the practical drawbacks associated with the so-called expansion of the reserved share cannot be ignored.
To this end, it is necessary to start from the consideration that the exercise of the action for reduction is subject to the ordinary ten-year limitation period and that there is no provision for an actio interrogatoria, unlike what happens with regard to the acceptance of inheritance (Article 481 of the Italian Civil Code). It follows that, at the opening of the succession, each legitimate heir may bring an action for reduction only with regard to the portion of the deceased's estate to which he or she would be entitled on the basis of the latter's family situation at that time. Only after the other legitimate heirs have waived their right to bring an action for reduction or after the limitation period has expired to their detriment may he or she take action to obtain a supplement to the legitimate portion, with obvious uncertainty in the meantime as to the fate of a portion of the assets that the deceased has disposed of by donation or will in favour of third parties.
Nor can any useful arguments in favour of the criticised thesis be inferred from Article 538 of the Civil Code. Firstly, in the reasoning transcribed above, the reference to a two-thirds share reserved for ascendants by Article 537 of the Civil Code is incomprehensible, since that provision refers to the share reserved for legitimate or natural children.
Furthermore, it is not clear why the conclusion (which would be reached by adhering to the argument that the court considers preferable) that, if the deceased's legitimate children survive and all renounce their inheritance, no right of legitimate inheritance would arise in favour of the ascendants, would be inadmissible. First of all, it should be noted that it is not clear whether the renunciation refers to the acceptance of the inheritance or to the bringing of an action for reduction.
In the first case, the issue of protecting ascendants would not even arise, as the legitimate succession pursuant to Article 569 of the Italian Civil Code would apply in their favour, since the legitimate children, having renounced their inheritance, would be considered as never having been called to succession.
In the second case, the exclusion of the possibility of a reserved share in favour of ascendants would be an expression of the legislator's choice to guarantee the acquisition of a share of the deceased's estate only to the closest relatives (as well as the spouse) existing at the time of the opening of the succession. Relatives of a subsequent degree, who are considered legitimate only in the absence of those of a closer degree, therefore, cannot be reinstated in the event of failure by the latter to exercise the right of reduction. Ultimately, the legislator considered it unfair for the deceased to dispose of his entire estate in favour of strangers if he had only descendants or only ascendants; However, it did not consider it unfair that the acts by which the deceased, who leaves descendants and ascendants, disposed of his entire estate in favour of strangers remain valid if the descendants (the only legitimate heirs considered) do not exercise the right of reduction.
In light of the above considerations, it can therefore be concluded that, for the purposes of determining the reserved portion due to the individual categories of legitimate heirs and to the individual legitimate heirs within the same category, reference must be made to the situation existing at the time of the opening of the succession and not to that which arises as a result of the failure (due to renunciation or prescription) of any of the legitimate heirs to bring an action for reduction'.
In doctrine, however, it has been noted that the above-mentioned orientation of the SSUU would apply only to cases of renunciation or prescription of the action for reduction, not to renunciation of inheritance, as in the present case (doc. 22 plaintiff's file), and this by emphasising Article 552 of the Civil Code as the key provision, which states: 'The legitimate heir (Articles 536 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code) who renounces the inheritance (Article 519 of the Italian Civil Code), when there is no representation (Article 467 of the Italian Civil Code), may retain the donations (Articles 769 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code) or obtain the legacies made to him (Article 521 of the Italian Civil Code) from the available portion; but when there has been no express waiver of imputation (Articles 553, 564 and 724 of the Italian Civil Code), if it is necessary to reduce (Article 553 et seq. of the Italian Civil Code) the testamentary dispositions or donations (Article 554 of the Italian Civil Code) in order to supplement the legitimate portion due to the heirs, the allocations made by the testator on the disposable portion, which would not be subject to reduction if the legitimate heir accepted the inheritance, remain unaffected, and the donations and legacies made to the latter are reduced"; in the Report of the Minister of Justice G.D. to the Civil Code of 4 April 1942, we read:
"One issue that I have re-examined is that of the fate of donations and legacies on account of the legitimate portion in the event of renunciation by the beneficiary. As is well known, the 1865 code provided in this regard that the renouncing party may retain the donation or claim the legacy up to the amount of the disposable portion, while he or she may not retain or obtain anything by way of legitimate portion. The provision, reproduced verbatim in Article 338 of the preliminary draft, was deleted in the final draft because it was considered superfluous, since in the new system, those who do not accept are not heirs, and only heirs are required to collate and are entitled to the legitimate portion. The accuracy of this principle with regard to the right to the legitimate portion has not been disputed. However, the opinion has been expressed that it would be preferable to reinstate the provision relating to the exemption from collation by the renouncing party, in order to avoid any doubt that he or she may retain the donation or claim the legacy even beyond the limit of the available portion. This proposal led me to re-examine the advisability of overcoming the traditional solution to the problem, which has been almost unanimously criticised by legal scholars. It has indeed been observed that the practical consequences of applying the provision of Article 1003 of the old code are often contrary to the foresight and wishes of the head of the family who has made assignments in anticipation of inheritance. In fact, the renunciation of succession by a child who has benefited from a donation on account of the legitimate portion increases the legitimate portion of the other children and may therefore result in a reduction in the gifts made by the deceased as disposable assets, which would not have been subject to reduction if the legitimate heir had accepted. I recognised these observations as fully justified and therefore considered it necessary to seek a different solution that would reconcile the following fundamental principles: a) respect for the wishes of the deceased, who, by making the donation on account of the legitimate portion, did not intend to preclude the possibility of allocating the disposable portion as he wished or to alter the situation of the other legitimate heirs; b) the principle that the renouncing party should not receive anything by way of legitimate portion; c) the principle that, since the renouncing party is considered extraneous to the inheritance, the other legitimate heirs must absorb the entire legitimate portion; d) the requirement that any beneficiaries of the disposable portion should not be at the mercy of the renouncing party. One possible system would have been to charge donations or legacies on account of the legitimate portion to the unavailable portion; but this system seemed incongruous to me, because it would have given the renouncing party an excessively advantageous position. In fact, the renouncing party could have retained the legitimate portion and the surplus on the disposable portion, whereas according to the rule of the 1865 code, they cannot retain anything as a legitimate portion. Another system I considered was to provide for the cancellation of any donation or bequest on account of the legitimate portion for the part corresponding to the legitimate portion; but I had to reject this solution as well because it would have the disadvantage of rescinding acts of generosity made within the family after some time, contrary to the presumed will of the disposer. I therefore decided to adopt a fourth system, according to which the renouncing heir may retain the donations or obtain the legacies made to him, on the disposable portion, provided that this does not prejudice the allocations made by the testator on the disposable portion that would not have been subject to reduction if the heir had come into the succession. Therefore, if it is necessary to reduce testamentary dispositions or gifts in order to supplement the legitimate portion due to the heirs, the allocations made by the deceased on the available portion, which would not have been affected if the renouncing heir had come into the succession, remain unaffected; on the other hand, the following are reduced donations and bequests made to the renouncing party. In essence, the order in which the action for reduction must be brought by the accepting heirs is changed, who must take action against the renouncing party, respecting the other allocations on the available estate. The fairness of this solution, which takes due account of the various requirements I mentioned above, does not seem to me to be questionable. According to this argument, the provision in question would therefore mean that, in the event of renunciation of the inheritance by the legitimate heir, the reserved shares of the other legitimate heirs would have to be recalculated, while the theory of the so-called 'crystallisation' of shares should be limited to cases of renunciation or prescription of the action for reduction.
In fact, in case law on the merits, applications of the principle of 'crystallisation' can also be found in cases of renunciation of inheritance (cf. Vicenza Court, 28/10/2021, no. 1976, DeJure); another court of first instance points out, in particular, that the renunciation of inheritance by the pretermitted heir would be without effect since the inheritance had not been opened in his favour: in particular, "... in the absence of a successful action for reduction, the renunciation by the pretermitted heir is without effect, as there is no share of the inheritance that remains unacquired as a result of the renunciation itself, given that in the case of a pretermitted heir, there is no inheritance in his favour. (r.g.a.c. no. 3491/2011, 3492/2011, 6156/2012). Therefore, in order to acquire the share due to the pretermitted heir, it is necessary to first successfully challenge the waiver of the action for reduction, which eliminates the effectiveness of the testamentary provisions that are detrimental to the rights of the pretermitted heir (...) Although the Court appears to have dealt only with the consequences of waiving the right to bring an action for reduction, there is no doubt that the same practical result can be achieved even in the case of renunciation of inheritance. Where, in fact, the person to whom the law reserves a share of the inheritance has only been prejudiced, by renouncing the (partial) inheritance in his favour, provided that the conditions for representation in favour of the descendants of the person renouncing the inheritance do not apply in relation to the amount of inheritance devolving to him by will or by legitimate succession, he will lose all inheritance rights and will also be precluded from bringing an action for reduction. r.g.a.c. no. 3491/2011, 3492/2011, 6156/2012 Similarly, the pretermitted heir, excluded from the inheritance, by renouncing the right to take legal action to reduce the prejudicial provisions, will no longer be able to obtain the share reserved for him by law and will lose the only possibility of claiming the inheritance of the deceased. In one way or another, the legitimate heir will not be included in the succession. Ultimately, the interpretation of the Supreme Court, in its enlarged composition, certainly has the merit of simplifying the calculation of the reserved share due to the legitimate heir, which becomes insensitive to subsequent events. The Court therefore considers it necessary to reiterate that if the deceased leaves a number of legitimate heirs who are harmed by donations or testamentary dispositions that exceed the available share, the failure of one of them to bring an action for reduction does not affect the share due to the others and does not increase it. Instead, it is the donee, heir or legatee who are the recipients of the detrimental provision, to benefit from the choice of the renouncing or inactive heir, in that, for the relevant share, they may retain the attribution in their favour. There is no reason to depart from this principle, given its consistency with the letter and purpose of the provisions..." (Court of Palermo, Section II, 17/07/2017, No. 3952; DeJure). Therefore, it must be considered that even in the case of renunciation of inheritance, it is not possible to deviate from the ruling of the SSSUU, given that the practical effect and the protection requirements underlying this case are similar to the case explicitly addressed by the Court.
These principles must then be coordinated with the testamentary nature of the inheritance in the case in question and with the need to respect the wishes of the deceased, as mentioned above. It is reiterated that the will reads as follows: 'I, the undersigned THE DECEASED, born in (OMISSIS), in full possession of my mental faculties, hereby dispose of my assets for the time when I am no longer alive: I appoint my children HEIR 4, HEIR 1, HEIR 2 and HEIR 3 as my heirs. I assign to my son HEIR 3 my disposable portion in addition to the reserve to which he is entitled. Forlì, 17 June 2007". The reserve due to all the children must be calculated in accordance with Article 542, paragraph 2, of the Italian Civil Code, by virtue of the aforementioned principle of crystallisation, since the deceased, at the time of her death, 'left' a husband and four children. The legitimate share of the latter is unaffected by subsequent events, so that RELATIVE 1's renunciation cannot determine the increase (hypothesis 1) or recalculation (hypothesis 3) of the shares of the children to whom THE DECEASED clearly intended to leave only the reserved share. The ideal share due to RELATIVE 1 can only be attributed to the available portion for a total of 4/8 (2/8 + 2/8 RELATIVE 1 share); therefore, the shares must be recalculated as follows: HEIR 2 1/8, HEIR 1 1/8, HEIR 4 1/8, HEIR 3 5/8 (equal to 1/8 + 2/8 + 2/8).
Finally, the following requests by HEIR 2 must be declared inadmissible, as they are new and were only proposed late in the clarification of the conclusions:
"ASSURE AND DECLARE that HEIR 3 violated Article 620 of the Italian Civil Code with regard to the failure to submit the holographic will to the notary for publication as soon as news of the testator's death was received, having concealed the holographic will of 6 September 2006 of the deceased THE DECEASED, who was already ill at the time but certainly capable of understanding and willing, a will published on 11 September 2018 by the notary THIRD PARTY 3 of Forlì; ASSURE AND DECLARE that the aforementioned HEIR 3 violated all duties of loyalty and integrity by publishing the holographic will of THE DECEASED dated 17 June 2007 late in 2013, concealing, on that occasion, the will dated 6 September 2006 and creating the conditions for the challenge - proposed by writ of summons for civil case no. 3958/17 r.g., relating to the division of the estates of RELATIVE 1 and THE DECEASED - given the incapacity to make a will of the aforementioned THE DECEASED two months before her death; for failing, in the face of the challenge to the aforementioned holographic will of 17 June 2007, to inform the judge and the undersigned plaintiff challenging the aforementioned will of 17 June 2007 of the existence of another will - of which the other two co-heirs were also aware, certainly HEIR 1, who was the first to produce it by filing it pursuant to Article 87 of the implementing provisions dated 6 September 2006, thereby causing the judge and the co-heir to mistakenly believe that the will of 17 June 2007 was the only will, acting in absolute bad faith and in violation of every duty of loyalty and integrity in hearing the case with regard to the will of 17 June 2007 - considering it more favourable to him than the will of 6 September 2006 - so that the investigating judge admitted evidence for formal questioning and for witnesses with regard to the mental condition of THE DECEASED on 17 June 2007".
With regard to the following questions from HEIR 2: "ASSURE AND DECLARE that the production of the holographic will of 6 September 2006 - null and void and ineffective for the reasons already expressed regarding the complete disposal of his estate by THE DECEASED, who was otherwise capable in September 2006 - in the course of the present case 3958/17 r.g. by means of a reconventio reconventionis is procedural conduct punishable on the basis of the case law of the Supreme Court, ex plurimis Cass. Civ., 12.09.2003, no. 13427, which states: "Pursuant to Article 92, paragraph 1, of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, the violation of the duty of loyalty and probity established by Article 88 of the aforementioned code justifies, regardless of the outcome of the case, the condemnation of the party that has failed to fulfil this duty to reimburse the legal costs that the other party has had to incur as a result of the unlawful conduct. Therefore, the judge does not violate the principle of liability for costs by ordering the winning party to pay the costs of the proceedings, where he or she finds - with discretionary assessment that cannot be reviewed on grounds of legitimacy, if adequately justified in relation to the logic and reality of the proceedings - that this was made necessary by the conduct of the winning party in violation of the aforementioned duty"; ASSURED that HEIR 1's involvement in the aforementioned conduct in violation of Article 88 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure is manifestly in bad faith, for having even filed a copy of the aforementioned will on 6 September 2006 after appearing in court with an irregular filing, these, being relevant to the costs of the proceedings, will be settled at the final stage.
That being established, the case must be remanded for the continuation of the preliminary investigation into the other claims.
Costs to be settled at the final stage.
